Pip the crow landed on the fence post and fixed Mara with one black eye. It had been, she decided, a ‘quiet’ morning until then.

‘You are late,’ Pip said.

“I didn’t know crows kept time,” Mara said, setting down her basket.

‘This one does,’ Pip told her, ‘and this one is hungry.’

Mara laughed. ‘Of course he is,’ she thought. The bread in her basket was meant for the ‘important’ guests, not for a bird with opinions.

“Is that bird talking again?” Tobin asked, coming round the corner of the barn.

“He never stops,” Mara said. She tore a corner off the loaf. ‘Just a little,’ she whispered, holding it out.

Pip snatched it and flapped up to the roof. From there he declared: ‘Fine bread. Poor company.’

Tobin read the note pinned to the barn door. ‘Back by noon.’ The ink had run in the rain, and the word ‘noon’ was barely there. He shrugged and called it a ‘sign’ of better things to come.
